options.text: It let Portuguese ships carry more soldiers and heavy cannon than any other ship of the time
options.misconception: Mixes up ship types; caravels were small and light, and the big gun-carrying ships were the carracks.

options.text: It let Portuguese ships sail without a compass or any other navigational instruments at all
options.misconception: Sails and instruments did different jobs; caravels still needed the compass and the astrolabe to navigate.

options.text: It let Portuguese ships sail home against the Atlantic winds instead of waiting for a favorable wind
It let Portuguese ships cross the Atlantic in a single day without stopping for supplies
options.misconception: No ship crossed the Atlantic in a day; the crossing took weeks even with good wind.

rationales.general:
1. Name the change. The lateen sail let a ship sail into the wind instead of only with it.
2. Picture the problem off Africa. Portuguese ships sailing south had to come home against the winds that pushed them down.
3. Ask what the old ships could do. Square sails ran well downwind but could not beat back up the coast.
4. Rule out the others. Caravels were small, slow to cross, and still needed instruments; their edge was the sail.
Remember: a new tool matters when it solves the exact problem the old tool could not.
rationales.C: Lateen sails let a ship sail close to the wind, so Portuguese crews could work their way home against the Atlantic winds instead of waiting months for a wind to turn.
rationales.A: Caravels were small and lightly armed; the big ships that carried heavy cannon were the carracks. Size and guns were not the caravel's edge.
rationales.B: A sail does not replace navigation. Caravel crews still used the compass, the astrolabe, and portolan charts to find their way.
rationales.D: No ship of the 1400s crossed the Atlantic in a day. The crossing took weeks, and the caravel's edge was sailing against the wind, not speed.

stem: The caravel's lateen sails let it sail against the wind, while the larger square-rigged ships of the time sailed best with the wind behind them. What does this difference best show about why the caravel mattered to Portuguese exploration?

stimulus.source_note: Engraving by Frans Huys after Pieter Bruegel the Elder, 16th century, public domain (Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0); text summarizes the Portuguese voyages down the African coast.
stimulus.text: Portuguese caravels crept down the African coast across the 1400s, each voyage pushing farther in search of a sea route to the spice markets of Asia. The engraving shows sailing ships of the 1500s with large triangular lateen sails, the sails that let caravels sail against the wind.
